utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we start, Mr. Forand, we have considered your travel arrangements. Unfortunately, we're not able to accommodate you as far as leaving today is concerned. I really feel sorry about that. At the very beginning of your testimony, I asked at a certain moment what your limitations were. We were then not informed about your plans, so we really feel sorry for you. At the same time, we have made some arrangements that we might need even today a bit of extra time, rather than to wait until Monday to find additional time today, so in order to make sure that at least your testimony will be concluded. We received a request from the Gotovina Defence for extra time; and I must say after a lot of hesitation, we at least arranged for one session this afternoon. I'm also aware that this might create some problems as far as the division of time between the Defence teams is concerned. The Defence teams are invited to try to find an arrangement for that. If you don't succeed, we'll have to consider whether or not to use this extra time; and if there is no agreement between the Defence teams, then also to consider how to resolve it, whether to grant the extra time or not. Arrangements are there, but I can imagine that other Defence teams will have to really fit into the allotted time that they might ask for a bit of that time as well. I leave it at this moment to the parties. If no agreement can be reached, the Chamber would like to be informed and then we'll decide the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have an agreement with Mr. Kuzmanic [sic], and Mr. Kuzmanic is going to, with the Court's permission, start today, if that's with Your Honour's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It saves time to call him, Mr. Kuzmanic instead of Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's my Brooklynese, Judge, which isn't translatable in UN parlance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed. Mr. Tieger, could you give us an indication of how much time you'd need for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think approximately 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Forty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as we can foresee now, the Chamber would need no more than ten to 15 minutes; so, therefore, the Defence teams are invited to leave approximately one hour at the end of the cross-examination for Mr. Tieger and for questions from the Bench. And if you think that this would cause a lot of further cross, then stop earlier with your cross. Mr. Kuzmanovic, please proceed. Mr. Forand, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I thank my colleagues for allowing me to proceed today. I hope to be done by the first break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General for, my name is Tom Kuzmanovic, I represent and am one of the attorneys for General Markac in this case. General, you arrived in July of 1995 in Sector South, and you were aware that the UN Security Council had several resolutions regarding your mandate that were handed down in 1994, UN Security Resolution 947 and UN Security Resolution 367, which basically spelled out your mandate; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact in P401, if you can pull that up, please, on page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do we have that up yet? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of page P401, which is your presentation of June of 1996, you describe what your tasks were at the very bottom of page 11: "To monitor and report on violations in the zone of separation, to monitor border crossing points, to protect Croats in 13 monitored villages, and promote confidence building measures." Now, at the time that you came to your sector, General, the Croats were the minority in your sector; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, most of these Croats, other than the ones that were left, had been forcibly removed before your arrival, correct, by the ARSK and JNA between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I cannot comment because I was not there, but the only Croat were left were those in those 13 monitored villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So, in essence, your job, as you described it, one of your jobs was to protect the Croats within your area of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between answer and question for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. My apologies. If we could go to page 9 of this same document, P401, and if we go toward the bottom of that document where the sentence begins, "The presence," and we'll go on into the next page, page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of this presentation, General, you had, when you got on the ground -- strike that. Confusing. When you got on the ground in July of 1995, you had described your organisational status by stating in -- on page 9 of P401: "The presence of UNMOs, UNCIVPOL, other UN organisations, and NGOs in the sector raises a particular problem. I had no operational control over any of these organisations and could not give them any order of direction, even though I had the sole responsibility of their security and the implementation of the cease-fire agreements. They reported and received directions and orders from their HQ in Zagreb. This situation created enormous friction, ambiguity, and coordination problems." Now, General, this was the situation in Sector South before Operation Storm; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it sounds strikingly similar to what was happening on the Croatian side after Operation Storm, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were various organisations that were entering the area afterwards; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the same organisations, sir. And I still had no operational control over them and I no longer had a mandate, as I explained, you know. It's in the sitrep where our task after Operation Storm was the dismantling of observation posts, recuperation of UN equipment; but at the same time, to raise any aspect, you know, that went against humanitarian rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, I understand that, but I guess the focus of my question was really that the Croatian side of the equation after Operation Storm had similar organisational problems in and of itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the Croatian organisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on what I was shown yesterday and the day before, yes, there seems to have been some problems within those organisations, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you a bit about what was going on in July in your sector before Operation Storm, and I'd like to point you to page 18 of P401, in this particular section, starting at where you say "secondly." You state that the: "Shocked by the easy defeat of Sector West, the Knin government reshuffled the Krajina Serb army, and called upon for aid from the Bosnian Serbs and Serbia. The requested assistance arrived in the form of retired Yugoslav National Army General Mile Mrksic, former commander of the Special Forces Corps. He also brought with him a cadre of Special Forces personnel, along with 4.000 veteran volunteers from other Yugoslav units." Now, this, General Forand, this reorganisation was occurring within your sector; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And all of this reorganisation and training and rearming was happening within the ambit of your area of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if all of those 4.000 volunteers, you know, were in Sector South or if they were distributed also in Sector North. What is reported here, I didn't see it myself. When I was looking for information for my presentation, that's what I was given by my staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. As a matter of fact, in your report, you say that: "He," being Mrksic, "was to oversee the reorganisation and modernization of the Krajina Serb army." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was told, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you, when you arrived in Sector South in July of 1995, were aware of what happened in Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I had seen the news in Canada before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And Srebrenica was a UN safe area as was the city of Bihac; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bihac, I couldn't tell you if it was a UN safe area. I know there was UN people there, but I'm not sure if it was a safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So, at least at this point, upon your arrival as far as you can recall in Sector South, you were not aware that Bihac was a UN safe area?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew there was some UN personnel there, but I don't recall if it was called a safe area, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand -- strike that. You further state on page 18 of P401 that: "His support," meaning Mrksic's support, "for the operation against the Bihac pocket may indicate he was trying to bolster that sector against what he anticipated would be Zagreb's next move." My question to you was: He was, meaning Mrksic's forces, were attacking the Bihac safe pocket from your area of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What he was doing, based on the information provided by my staff, was to move some of his military personnel from Sector South to the Bihac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they went there with -- they didn't go there with rocks and sticks, they went there with tanks and artillery and guns; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. You know, again, this is information that was passed to me by my staff when I was preparing that presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. You would agree with me, General, that Bihac is in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is a country separate and apart from Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And as part of your role in UN Sector South, you were to monitor the border, the internationally-recognised border, between Croatia and Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had only four border crossing points. If they passed outside of those border crossing points, there is no way for me to monitor that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but my question was: One of your responsibilities was to monitor the international border; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only at those four border crossing points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, General, that the ARSK troops, under Mrksic's command in combination with the Bosnian Serb army and other JNA forces, were using, in part, your area of responsibility to attack the UN safe area of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know or you don't recall?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, one of your responsibilities was to monitor heavy weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you have had several sitreps prior to Operation Storm in which you discuss the issue of Sector South's inability to monitor heavy weapon sites of the Bosnian Serbs, do you not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to recall that that was one of the problems where the ARSK had taken out their heavy weapon out of the sites, but I'm not so sure if it was my responsibility or if it was not the United Nations Military Observer's responsibility to monitor those heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at P337, please. Page 6, P337.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is one of your sitreps, General. If you look at the bottom of the sitrep, the bottom third --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: August 1st, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Three days -- four days before Operation Storm. Restriction of movements, at the bottom, point 6: "Access is still denied for inspection of all weapons storage sites."

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't just on August 1st, as reflected in P337, it was reflected in 65 ter 3122, if you could pull that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I would have used an exhibit number for this; however, I could not find this particular 65 ter number on the list of exhibits that was provided to us, and I don't know if that was just my inability to read or an omission. But the bottom of that particular -- on Annex B, 1361 is the page reference. 0090-1361. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That shows up as D164, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. D164.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, August 2nd, 1995, another sitrep from your sector, General, showing, again: "Access is still denied for inspection of all weapons storage sites." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But I would like to see the mandate of the military observer. In my mind, I think they were the one responsible for those monitoring of these heavy weapons. And as I mentioned, I think at the beginning of my points for the Prosecutor, that since we were receiving information from the military observer, some of those information also found itself in my daily sitrep. So that may have come from them, but I would have to look at the -- what was their mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Understanding that, General, it really -- had you had that mandate or had UNMO had that mandate, it really doesn't make a difference because access was denied; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can go back to P337 for a moment, and the same page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can go up, right where it says "Strmica" there, in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There's noted toward the right: "3 S Galeb fired three rockets into BH," and this is before Operation Storm; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And those are Serb aircraft firing rockets into BH; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Must be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P339, please, page -- I'll give you the -- it looks like a bates number, 0090-1592.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is another Sector South sitrep, dated 3rd of August of 1995, the day before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And under 2, General Situation, if we could highlight that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It says, "The general situation in Sector South remains tense. Activity at Strmica continued and was punctuated by the two RSK Super Galebs, which overflew Knin at 1710 hours, on their way to drop bombs in the area of Budim." Now, at this particular situation, this is the day before Operation Storm, there's Serb aircraft active, bombing what are presumably Croatian positions; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to page 5 of that sitrep, General. Under section D, can you explain to me, it says, "CanBat 1 ..." -- these are the battalion near Benkovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "... continues planning and preparation for they eventualities of the refugees in the AOR." Do you know who notified CanBat 1 that there might be refugees in the AOR on the day before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether -- I'll strike that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And again at the bottom of that page, in point 6: "Access is still denied for inspection of all weapons storage sites." Now, General, we don't have the sitreps at least in a dossier for us, and I'm sure they exist before August 1st, but would you agree with me that point number 6 was probably a broken record as far as you were concerned in terms of access for inspection of all weapons storage sites of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to talk to you a little bit more about Bihac, General. There were probably 70.000 to 80.000 people, if not more, in that pocket?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not familiar with Bihac at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me, General, that had the ARSK and the Bosnian Serb army been successful in taking the UN safe area of Bihac, partially using your area of responsibility as a base of operations, that there existed the real possibility of another Srebrenica had it been overrun?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm afraid, given the previous question, I have to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I was listening to the French translation and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to the French translation, and then it comes a bit late to me. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The previous question sought some information about Bihac, the witness indicated lack of familiarity with Bihac at all, and now there's further questioning about the impact of actions in Bihac. I don't think there's much basis for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, any reason to believe that the witness gained additional information on Bihac in the last five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sure, Your Honour. I can go back to P401.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not forget, if we are talking about the presentation, that the basis of knowledge and sometimes the opinions expressed in it, of course, is not the same as what we elicit as evidence from a witness. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You were critical of Mrksic for diverting resources in your presentation to Bihac; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say critical. To me, you know, it was a -- I could not understand why he was sending troops to Bihac while he was not improving his defensive position. That's an observation that I was making in my presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that by taking the area of Bihac, that the Serbs then would have had a contiguous land mass directly from Serbia through Bosnia all the way to Croatia and would have alleviated any situation with the loss of Bosansko Grahovo for supply line?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have been easier for them, yes, to resupply, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You said, in your report at page 20, that you thought that the results of Operation Storm may have been different in two scenarios: One, if General Mrksic had foregone the attack on Bihac and instead continued to use your area of responsibility as a base to set up defensive operations; or, had the RSK leadership not ordered the withdrawal of the civilian population of Sector South. Those were the two alternatives you presented; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's observation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, there was a withdrawal of the civilian -- ordered withdrawal of the civilian population of Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you further explain that that withdrawal was passed down to civilians by the RSK civil defence organisation?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I understood from conversation with the displaced people in my camp, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that RSK civil defence organisation was a remnant of the old Communist system; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was explained, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be repetitious. The witness explained that clearly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, General, you had some black-marketeering going on in your area of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the problems I was facing, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Hill, in his May 1997 statement, which is P292, discussed that in some sectors, there was a million litres of fuel a month that had gone missing. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that fuel was one of the commodity that was used for black-marketing. And as soon as I learned about it, I asked that they verify the mileage compared to the amount of gas that was given, and I restricted the amount of gas given to a certain unit to the mileage that they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you discover who was doing the black-marketing?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't discover the individual, but I knew that it was a particular unit, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was fuel that was being sold to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to Operation Storm specifically, General; and, again, referring to P401, page 20. First paragraph, you note --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll wait until it comes up. Thank you. I'm sorry. Page 20 of 45, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In that first paragraph, General, you note, in the latter part of that paragraph: "Their use," meaning the Croatian's use, "of artillery was excellent." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And there's nothing in that particular section that discusses anything about indiscriminate shelling of civilian targets, is there?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You also note that you had to recognise, in the next paragraph, that: "The Croatians had tremendous strategic success and that their small special force units did successfully accomplish special missions." And as a matter of fact, you had written to General Gotovina on August 26th of 1995 specifically asking about these special force units; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had asked him if he could provide me some information because I was preparing that presentation, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go to P375, please. Actually, at the bottom, it says "2/3 of P375." We'll use the bottom third, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Here, in the final paragraph, you request assistance in obtaining a historical appreciation of the military actions undertaken by the HV during Operation Storm. And in the last sentence of the paragraph, you state: "One particular area is the spectacularly successful seizing of the crossing of the Velebits from Obrovac to Mali Alan to Lovinac, the restoration of the road across that terrain," and if you go to the next page "and the subsequent operations towards Medak and Gracac." And you even ask, in the next paragraph, that you would be grateful if your officer who was preparing the briefing could be given a tour of this battlefield in the company of an English speaking officer, "who could also explain the plan and execution of what seems to be a bold and crucial part of the plan of attack for Operation Storm." Did you ever get that field briefing of the -- of that particular operation, General?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Gracac is one of the cities that's mentioned in P375. I'd like you to refer to the protest letter that you sent to General Gotovina on the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could pull that up, that's P83.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The first sentence of that letter protests the -- what is termed "unprovoked artillery attack on Knin and the towns of Drnis, Medak, Bunic, Benkovac, and Kistanje." Gracac is not listed in that letter, is it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, if we could pull up P307 on the screen, and if we could enlarge it just a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The centre circle is Gracac, is it not, General Forand?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot read on my --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we go a little closer if we can, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And as far as you were concerned, from your perspective, that was a strategically important place, given the fact that it had all of these intersections of important roads that went through it; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, essentially, from the right there, where the city of Otric is circled all the way across which would be west off the screen to the city of Gospic, was that particular road that eventually led into Knin; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the map, but yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we enlarge the map just for the benefit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly requested to pause between question and answer for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see, General, in the upper left-hand corner, the city of Gospic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your word for it because it's too small for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We can enlarge in, General. You see it there?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I is see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the left. Okay. Now, General, Gospic, as far as you knew at the time before Operation Storm, was a city that was essentially in Croatian hands; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At this time, I'd like to play 3D00-0857. It's a radio broadcast of August 4th, 1995 from CBC Radio One.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask at certain points that the broadcast be stopped because I am going to ask you some questions, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's stop for a moment. We get kind of an echo with a delay of up to ten or 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wanted to prove that I was right. Could the technicians in any way assist us? The echo seems to have been gone. Could we try again to play the audio. Have you provided the booth with a transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long is the part you wanted to play, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, with this quality of sound, we would survive that for 20 seconds but not for three minutes. The technicians are trying to find out what the problem is. Once they have any report on that, perhaps you can move on, then -

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will move on to a separate section. Your Honour, I will say that we listened to this, and it was perfectly fine on our system and I don't understand. It happened yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Neither do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll move on to a different section, General. I'd like to go over your statement, P330, page 10. Do you have your statement in front of you, General?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it the one from 1996 or 1997?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you can turn to page 10, please. I'll wait until it gets up on the screen. There is a paragraph that starts, "Within weeks," towards the top of your statement.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that's, I'm assuming, within weeks of Operation Storm; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You state: "The HV and Special Police units were going over some towns for the second time. They were burning houses that had already been almost totally destroyed." My question for you, General, is: First of all, did you ever see this occurring, the HV and Special Police units going over some towns for the second time?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it personally myself, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, what Special Police units are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to refer -- I don't think it was identified specifically. It was passed on to me, again, from my staff, and it must be listed in certain sitreps that was sent to UNCRO. But I don't remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So you have no specific personal knowledge of what Special Police units are referred to here?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I take it, then, that you don't know how the Special Police itself was structured?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know how the civilian police was structured?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You say, "within weeks," but are there any specific dates you can give us as to when this occurred that you referred to in P330?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe not for that specific, but I think our sitrep goes until the end of August where we still report that there are some burning taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm most interested in is the identification of who or what these HV and Special Police units were, and what you're telling us is that you can't help us there?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what kind of uniforms these units were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not tell you, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Later in that statement, in the following paragraph, you state, in the middle of the paragraph: "Sometimes heavy cordons of Croatian Special Police would block off an area." I wanted to ask you some questions about that. Did you personally see that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So, again, you wouldn't be able to tell us what units they were, what their uniforms were, whether they were civilian, military, or otherwise; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Similarly with that, there are no dates and no places that you could identify for us; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to refer back to the sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the rest of my questions, Your Honour, pertain to two radio broadcasts, the first of which we couldn't hear, the second of which is a little bit longer. And then I will be done with my questioning, so hopefully we can have this resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we hear from the technical booth, first of all, whether the problem has been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have several possibilities. One of them is to use different equipment to have it played. That's what we are trying now. And if that doesn't help us out, there's still the possibility that if there's a transcript, that the transcript will be read into the record, and that at a later stage, the parties have the possibility to verify whether the transcript reflects the original. But let's first see whether -- Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ms. Henry-Frijlink is trying it, Your Honour, but she has just logged on. So it will be just a minute until the computer activates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then wait for that possible solution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't want to -- I know specifically where I want to stop and ask questions; and if it would be all right with Alan if Randy Vlado could sit with Donnica, that way she doesn't not have do what is really our job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, in this urgent situation, the parties coming closer to each other, but Chamber is still aware what bears what responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could ask a couple of other questions until we get to this, so we don't waste time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can do that, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could call up P400.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General, if we could focus on the third paragraph, please. Now, in the third paragraph, there's a discussion of how many people left Sector South, and it's listed as 85.000 people. General, I'd like to -- the initial assessment, at least as shortly after Operation Storm was in your entire sector, there were 30.000 to 40.000 people prior to Operation Storm, meaning Serb civilians, and I'd like to know how that number began to grow two months later to 85.000 people from specifically in your sector, and to some point now we've got estimates by some Serbian politicians where it's 285.000 people. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A lot of factors, Your Honour, but with respect to the part of the predicate for the question, that is the initial assessment, at least as shortly -- I think the witness at least would need some information about the source of that initial assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please give the source. "The initial assessment ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's in the radio transcript, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's being given by General Forand himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember that, Mr. Forand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Which figure are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about the initial assessment of 30.000 to 40.000 people, Serb civilians, being present prior to Operation Storm, and may I take it in the whole of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just in his Sector South, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in his Sector South. Did you ever give such an initial assessment of 30.000 to 40.000 people, civilians, Serb civilians, in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it's in the transcript, obviously I did say that; but there is a report on a is sitrep that at one border crossing point, there was close to 77.000 or 78.000 people that passed there. And the figures that I was using at the end was in Sector South. There was close to 80.000 people, and some 78.000 people had left Sector South and there was about from 15 to 2.000 [sic] people that were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, General, you were aware that, at least at that particular checkpoint, those were people leaving from both Sector North and Sector South, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are we ready to try the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's give it a try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "CBC Radio One, As it Happens" "Hello, I'm Pamela Wallen, sitting in for Michael Enright." "Good evening, I'm Beth Gaines, sitting in for Barbara Budd. This is At It Happens." "Tonight, the Croatian government sends its troops to reclaim disputed territory from the Serbs; but for the UN peacekeepers, it's the same old hazard in a new location." "As It Happens, the Friday Edition: Radio that shifts gears with its feet." The Croatian government is calling it a police action. Everyone else is calling it a war. At 5.00 this morning, government forces attacked the Krajina region in an effort to wrest control of the area from rebel Croatian Serbs. The Serbs seized the Krajina region with the help of the Yugoslav army when Croatia declared independence four years ago. The town of Knin, which the Serbs have proclaimed as their capital, has been taking a pounding. Canadian Brigadier-General Alain Forand is the UN commander of the area. We reached him at his headquarters in Knin." "General Forand, you and your UN troops, the Canadian troops, are right in the middle of all of this." "Yes, unfortunately. And for the last hour, it has been fairly quiet, no more explosion in the town of Knin. But, today, I think there must have been somewhere around 700 to 800 shells throughout the cities; and also on the Canadian side because they are a small contingent here, and one is the Canadian one. We had three OP which were occupied forcibly by the Croats; but, fortunately, I am told that all the Canadians are safe, and they are presently at Zadar, which is a Croatian city on the Dalmatian coast."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask at this point to have it stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General Forand, I would like to go over with you that statement that you gave on the 4th of August regarding the number of shells. You stated that: "Somewhere around 700 to 800 shells throughout the cities ..." Now, that's the entire amount of shelling for that day throughout the cities, not just Knin, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in my mind, it was Knin that I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the -- at least what it sounds like to me is that you were referring to more than one city in that discussion?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have said 700 or 800 rounds, because the only place I was on that day was in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But you were receiving reports from others, were you not, about --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was receiving reports from the others; but in my mind, you know, 700 and 800 was in Knin. So English is not my first language, so if I said "cities," then I made a mistake. To me, I was referring to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we continue on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "There are not any injuries at this point that you know of?" "At this point, there is no injury, but the battle is still raging on in what is called the zone of separation. There are some gains that the Croats have made in the northern part of my sector and also in the middle of the sector. And there is a part of my is sector that I don't know have any news since approximately 12.00 today because of bad communication, and I suspect also that some of my people have been seized by the Croats in that particular area." "What are you doing all day long? What can you do, General? Are you really confined to your headquarters there? Is there any activity on the street?" "We have all kinds of problem here with restriction of movement, the shelling that was also occurring, you know, close to our base. And as a matter of fact, we received a couple of rounds on the base itself, but nobody was hurt. And I just got back from a meeting where we were discussing the evacuation of all the civilian population in Sector South." "Will you be in charge of that?" "Well, first, I cannot decide that, you know. It has to be the UN that agrees to that particular withdrawal plan, because we're talking about the evacuation of all the civilian population in my sector, which is around, you know, from 32.000 to 40.000 people."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, General, at least as of this date, August 4th, your estimate of the civilian population which was going to be withdrawn, the entire civilian population in your sector, was 32.000 to 40.000 people; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we continue then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "Do you know whether there are civilian casualties; and if there are, what can you do?" "Well, there are some civilian casualties. We had to evacuate some of them because we have some military ambulance. And when we were patrolling the towns and when we saw the people had been hit, you know, we put them in the vehicles and we bring them to the civilian hospital. There is, as I mentioned, there is a lot of area that, unfortunately, we were not allowed by the Serbs to go for military reasons, and we know that there have been some wounded and some dead, but it's difficult to assess the number presently."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you a question about that particular passage. You said you were not allowed by the Serbs to go for military reasons. What was that all about?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But you did specifically say you were not allowed by the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "It's been difficult to tell just what the international community's position is. Certainly some dire warnings from people like President Clinton this week, asking the Croats not to do this. But earlier on, I guess a bit of a mixed message. Where do you think we are now?" "Well, I think, you know, maybe militarily, I would say that the Serbs are really weakened presently. Even though they have shown extreme restraint, they have not used their artillery to fire on civilian cities, which the Croats did. The Croats, you know, bombarded all the Knin, the capital here, and all the small cities and towns around the edge of the zone of separation." "Thanks for talking with us tonight. Good luck." "Thank you, ma'am. Good night." "Canadian Brigadier-General Alain Forand spoke to us from Knin, Croatia. He's the United Nations Commander for Sector South."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could I please get a number for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D328.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D328 is admitted into evidence, and it's an audio recording plus transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General Forand, I wanted to ask you about that last passage where you say the Serbs have not used their artillery to fire on civilian cities, which the Croats did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the music and the good morning will remain on my mind, but also the remainder of the recording. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, that's probably the start of the second passage, but we're not there, Your Honour. If we could pull up P343, please, page 2. Actually, why don't we leave page 1 for a second, so we can orient the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a Sector South Knin HQ sitrep dated August 4th of 1995 at 2300 hours; correct, General?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we go to page 2, please. That's page 3. This might have been the one where they were input out of order. So it could be page 5, I'm being told, 5 of the document but page 2 on mine. That's it. We can see on the top, it says, "page 2," but it's actually page 5 of P343.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go toward the bottom of this page, General, this is your sitrep, meaning your HQ sitrep. And underneath the box - if we could highlight "Both sides" - it says: "Both sides are continuing artillery shelling over all Sector South areas of responsibility." And the third insert there is that two black aircraft were reported bombing Gospic. Now, Gospic is a Croatian city; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And at least by this sitrep, the Serbs weren't necessarily using restraint because both sides were continuing artillery shelling, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this sitrep, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, at the bottom of that page. Actually, that's not it. We'll forgo that. If we could go to page 7, which is the top page designation of 343.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you take a look under "military info assessment," General, the second to last sentence says: "It is assessed that ARSK forces will fight spirited resistance in small pockets, even if there is a general ARSK surrender or evacuation." That was the military assessment of whom?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That must have been Captain Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So, at least as of your radio broadcast, the Serbs did use artillery fire and aircraft fire on Croatian civilian areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the aircraft seen, it was reported, I don't know if it was ever verified; and the artillery shelling, I didn't say it was not said in the sitrep that the Serb shelling was shelling cities in the Croatian area. And I don't know what time I made that interview with CBC, what time it was, because this sitrep is at 2300. So more information may have been coming than I possessed when I spoke to that reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could pull up Exhibit D5, please, and the point 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is an UNMO document from UNMO HQ Sector South, dated 4 August 1995 at 1610, and it describes about Otocac continuously having artillery shelling ongoing. Otocac was a place that was in Croatian hands; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to the next page of that document, point 8, we've got UNMO team Gospic reporting that the explosion rate has been reduced to one per minute, meaning that there was artillery fire going on in Gospic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to be the case, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And Gospic is another city that was in Croatian hands at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now if we could pull up 65 ter 4695.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is another UNMO sitrep, dated 5 August, day two of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And if we could focus in on the lower third of that where it begins "ARSK arty," and if we could move that up. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "ARSK arty attacked several Croatian towns like Gospic, Sibenik, Vodice, Otocac. Otocac was also attacked by Serb aviation." Then later there, it says: "ARSK attempted to hit Zagreb with Luna rocket, but the fire was too short." So the Serbs were attacking Croatian civilian towns with artillery, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what a Luna rocket is, General?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This 65 ter I believe is an exhibit but I could not find the exhibit number, Your Honour, and I will endeavour to do my best to find one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it has no exhibit number, then we'll assign it, if Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm afraid all our stations are being used at the moment, Your Honour. So we can't check or verify that one way or another, but we'll try to do so at the earliest opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to find that in a dossier, the UNMO dossier, but I couldn't find it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's keep on the safe side. Mr. Registrar, this would be exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be Exhibit D329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's no objection. I don't know if someone has discovered a previous exhibit number or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I've been told the P104, Your Honour, and I'm thankful for my colleague to pass that on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, the number is now vacated again, and we'll check whether P104 is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I say "vacated," of course, it's free again to be used for another exhibit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. The last area of questioning I have resolves around the second radio broadcast. That's 3D00-0840. The original was over 20 minutes long. I know that that wasn't something that was feasible. We cut it down to what we believe is a reasonable six to seven minutes, and the transcripts have been provided, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please play the audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Hello, good morning, and welcome to Sounds Like Canada for Monday, July the 21st. I'm Sheila Cole, siting in one last week for Sheila Rogers." "When we think of the war in Yugoslavia, the images that come to mind for most ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "July the 21st. I'm Sheila Cole, sitting in last week for Sheila Rogers."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for reference, this is July 21st of 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "When we think of the war in Yugoslavia, the images that come to mind for most people are of Serb massacres. But for many Canadian soldiers who lived that war, the defining memory is of Croatian atrocities. Eight hundred Canadians went as peacekeepers to Croatia in 1995. They ended up as witnesses to an orgy of killing and looting. Now they want to testify about those crimes at The Hague. The CBC's Evan Dyer has been talking with some of the soldiers, and he joins us now from our studio in Ottawa. "Good morning, Evan." "Good morning, Sheila." "Well, let's go back to 1995, and set the scene for us. What was happening in Croatia at the time?" "Well, that vicious civil war between Serbs and Croats was in its last year. The war in Bosnia, of course, still going very strong, but the Croatian war had been pretty much dormant for about two years. However, the Croats had never given up on the idea of reconquering the Serb-held areas of Croatia where the Canadians were based. Most of all, they wanted at that take back the Krajina which was a strip of land which for centuries really had been mostly Serbian. And the Canadian army had been there since about 1992 over three years, trying to defend the people in the Krajina, both Serbs and Croats. I talked to Major-General Alain Forand of the Canadian army. He was the commander of the UN forces in the area, and he says the world didn't have a lot of sympathy for the Serbs that he was protecting." "We should remember those days, you know, the bad guys was the Serbs. CNN was not in Croatia. There was almost no news, you know, coming out of Croatia, and whatever was coming out of was they got what they deserve. And all of a sudden, you know, they lose the little that they had, and they are sent to one of those God-forsaken places in Serbia with nothing left, and what's their hope, you know, for life? It's almost nothing but, Well it's the Serbs, they deserve it. Everybody forgot about it very quickly." "Now, this plan to expel the Serbs was code named Operation Storm. It's the operation we are talking about. Essentially, it was a shock and awe type of blitzkrieg operation, very aptly named because it began with this just ferocious, by all accounts, artillery bombardment, which far exceeded what anyone thought the Croats were capable of. And that barrage rolled right over the UN line of separation and the bunkers of the Canadian forces." "Now, the Canadians are talking about war crimes. What was it they saw?" "Well, the first war crime actually is the shelling itself. And I spoke about this with Major-General Andrew Leslie. Now he's off to next week to Afghanistan. Actually, he's going to be the commander of the Canadian forces there. But back then, in 1995, he was the colonel in the Krajina capital of Knin." "I'm a gunner, I'm an artillery officer, a professional, so I can comment on it with some degree of validity. This was deliberate targeting on a massive scale of residential areas. Why? Because I believe it was targeted to break their will to resist. And by the way, it worked. It killed a lot of civilians, and we'll never know the exact number. But estimates, estimates range from 10 to 25.000 dead."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the transcript says "dead after 10 to 25.000."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "It worked. It killed a lot of civilians, and we'll never know the exact number. But estimates, estimates range to 10 to 25.000 dead."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I just want to let that soak in again for a minute there, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, General Forand, for someone in the year 2003, eight years after Operation Storm, to make this kind of a statement on a national radio broadcast, that 10 to 25.000 civilians were killed as a result of the shelling of Knin, is not just I remember responsible, it's a complete fabrication, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you asking me? I'm not General Leslie. I didn't make that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You were his commander, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. And you and he were there at the same time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I was not at the same time with him when he made that declaration on that radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you there were not 10 to 25.000 civilians killed as a result of the shelling in Knin, General; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no, and I never used that figure, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General Leslie did though; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem according to that transcript, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, it's clear what the testimony is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If Milan Martic would have said that, you would have called him a liar, would you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "25.000, and this absolutely indiscriminate. We're talking from small children to old people here?" "The shelling was aimed basically at houses, and it moved across the town from one end to the other, a hospital also, everything in the town. But not just in Knin, every town in the Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General, the hospital was not a target of the shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that there was a hit on the hospital. I never verified it myself, but that's what I was told. But I don't think it was a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General, you would agree with me that the shelling in Knin was not aimed at houses, was it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my point of view, as I explained the other day, it seems that it was -- that the shell were landing all over Knin. So I don't know how you would qualify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that houses were not being aimed at in Knin or any other town in Krajina specifically; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my point of view, again, when I was on that balcony, what I was looking at, it was falling all over the place where there were some civilian house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we move on to the next passage, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "And the Croats, in fact, had total control of Krajina within about four days. But as the General says, the killing didn't end there; and, in fact, it was really just getting started. And General Leslie says he saw Croatian police afterwards going house to house and killing anyone they found." "There were a variety of organisations that then swept into the former Serbian Krajina. There were Special Police teams, wearing their very distinctive blue uniforms, who were engaged in hunting and killing in the mountains of Serbian civilians. And I saw dozens and dozens of farm houses and even villages burning, many, many days, in some cases months, after the initial assault had taken place."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, General Forand, General Leslie left Knin for good on August 7th, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next portion, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "So did you succeed in getting some documentation; and, of course, there's what they saw, their accounts. What happens or what is happening with their depositions to The Hague?" "Not very much actually. There's not really enough happening. There has been one indictment, but there's been absolutely no arrests, and the Canadians are quite frustrated about it. Here is General Forand." "Well, that's the sad part in a sense, you know, that I made a deposition, you know, on what I had seen, that people were dead, and the looting and all the things. So I made the deposition. Lo and behold, seven, eight months after that, another group came from the Tribunal because they told me that they had lost my deposition. So I made another one. And would you believe that they came back a third time, another group, because somebody within the organisation again had lost everything I had made. So I made a third one, and I said, "Well, this time, you better keep it because otherwise don't come and see me again." But I never heard from these people. I'm still waiting for the news. I don't know." "And he must be dealing with an incredible level of frustration as well." "After eight years, yes." "Yeah. So what are we talking about? Who are these alleged war criminals?" "Well, two of them are dead. President Franjo Tudjman is one of them. He died in his bed. So did the other general named in the indictment. But one remains alive and in hiding, General Ante Gotovina. I should tell you about this guy. He's got quite a history. General Ante Gotovina is a former Foreign Legionnaire, French Foreign Legionnaire; Commander of Operation Storm; one of the only Croatians in the Croatian army ever to be indicted. But the Croatian government has been very reluctant to hand him over; and, actually, he just went out and hired him a lawyer, in fact. And the fact that General Gotovina remains unpunished continues to annoy Canadian officers like General Leslie." "Well, I can't see how anybody could survive for so long in a relatively small chunk of grounds, which is what Croatia is - I mean, we have lakes that are bigger than Croatia, for goodness sake - without assistance from the local population. There's a good many Croats who believe he's a national hero."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, why don't we just proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "Why hasn't the West been more aggressive in his pursuit?" "That's a good question, because of course the West put crushing sanctions on Serbia to force it to turnover its war criminals. And now it's aggressively pursuing them, and, you know, it sent one over in just recent weeks. But Croatia, on the other hand, is on the short list to join the European Union, to join NATO. Now it's going to Iraq. It's very close to the United States. I think, you know, the answer is that the world is not putting pressure on Croatia partly because the West in 1995 was on the Croatian side. And, you know, everybody at this point has identified the Serbs as the problem, and, you know, they had committed terrible atrocities just before Storm in Bosnia. Srebrenica was just a few weeks before. And once you identify the Serbs as the problem, it was a short step for some countries, like the US and Germany in particular, to identify the Croats as the solution. One of the ironies of Yugoslavia is that peace when it finally became possible, and it was possible partly because the ethnic cleansing had been so successful. And the Croats weren't going to make peace as long as the Serbs remained in control of the Krajina." "So you are talking about with actual assistance from the West? "Well, it's, you know, the West was definitely aiding the Croatians, in the sense that they were getting vehicles from Germany, artillery from Argentina, training from the United States. And every officer I spoke to believes that the Croatian army received foreign assistance, mostly directly in Operation Storm, because they believe Operation Storm was too good, too professional, really, for an army run by a bunch of former Croatian policemen. Here is General Leslie." "The coordination of the fires, the psychological preparation of the battlefields had to have been done by people who really knew what they were doing. I can't see what where they would have pulled off the expertise to get it done."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General Forand, I wanted to ask you a question about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, one second for taking a breath for the interpreters and transcribers, and then we can slowly proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll count to five, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General, I wanted to ask you a question about that last passage and comment of General Leslie's, and you also were of the opinion, to some extent, that you didn't understand where the Croatian military would have pulled off the expertise to get this done; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite put it like that, but yes, that was in the back of my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I guess, is it me or does it seem like you want to have it both ways? In one sense, they had too much expertise to pull -- they did not have enough expertise to pull this off and do it so well; and on the other hand, they are a bunch of unprofessional former policemen. Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Was this a professional military operation undertaken by the Croatian military, or was this just some rag tag operation where they got lucky?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, if you read my presentation, I do both, you know. I say, strategically, it was very well planned. There was some parts which were very well done; but in other parts, there seemed to be a lacking of a cooperation between the combat arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we move on with the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "So who are these people who really knew what they were doing?" "Well, there is a company in Alexandria, Virginia called Military Professional Resources Inc., MPRI. And it's always been very open about the fact that it was training the Croatian army before Storm; significantly, before Storm. It's currently arming the Croatian arm now for NATO, in fact. MPRI is a company that's a very, very close to the Pentagon. And the president of the MPRI, Carl Vuono, is non-other than the former Chief of Staff to the United States Army. General Vuono was in Croatia with the Croatian General Staff in the days immediately prior to Storm, just a couple of days before. And we know that MPRI at that point was training the Croatian army. I think the question a lot of people in the Canadian army are curious about, and I have to say that no one here I spoke to claims to know the definitive answer to this, is how directly did MPRI and the US help with Operation Storm. For example, you know, did they provide intelligence? Did they go so far as to help the draft the actual plan of attack? You know, the Americans had satellite and aerial images of the battlefield. Did the Croatian army use those to target the refugee columns, for example. I know there's a lot of Canadian officers who think the that answers to some of those questions at least is, yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General, after listening to that last passage, are you one of those Canadian officers who thinks the answers to some of those questions is yes?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You are?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. I would like to move this particular transcript into evidence, along with the audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. Just in keeping with the point made yesterday, if I understood Mr. Kuzmanovic correctly, these were -- sounded like the entire broadcast, but I thought I understood him earlier to say that it was an excerpted portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We did excerpt it. I'll get you the whole thing. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this becomes Exhibit D329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D329 is admitted into evidence. That's an audio with transcript. Mr. Kuzmanovic, just one question. This was not put to Mr. Leslie when he testified, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wish I had it then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wish I had it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I refrain from commenting on it, which is appropriate, I think. I was just verifying whether my recollection was right or wrong. Then, just for us to know, this concludes your cross-examination, which means that now who is next? Mr. Kehoe, you will be the next one after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how much time are you planning to use?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will -- I understand that I will endeavour to -- I will finish with an hour left, 45 minutes for the Prosecution and I guess the 15 minutes the Court has, but I do have a significant amount of information to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's always the answer. It's like -- no, well, let's not. Could you tell us how much time you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me chat just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, General, by the way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would say two and a half hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any agreement with the Cermak Defence, because they were limited in their time; and as I said before, if additional time is available, then, of course, we have to consider whether it would be fair to grant extra time to those counsel who have stayed well within the limits the Chamber has set.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, what I've done is concluded matters on Your Honour's suggestion with those bundles of documents, which I would have been putting in the way that Your Honour and the Court had a flavour of, and that that was the purpose of that. Those are being prepared and will be available for distribution at some point this morning. They are being printed and scheduled, and trying to make as much as possible that the right 65 ter number -- well they're all right 65 ter numbers, but the operative 65 ter number is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer well that you're not claiming at this time any of the extra time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not claiming, Your Honour, because I've done my piece on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you can use two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not two hours and 31 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Forand, you know Mr. Kehoe already, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've had that pleasure, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
