utterances.text: Then, Mr. Tieger, are you ready to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Forand. I now have the opportunity to raise briefly with you some of the matters that were touched upon during cross-examination. The first one that I'd like to address concerns an issue that was raised by Mr. Kay, and that is your first meeting with General Gotovina on August 8th. And you were questioned about that beginning, for the benefit of my colleagues and perhaps you'll want a chance to look at that portion of the transcript as well, at page 4199. Actually, excuse me, beginning -- I think the questioning began earlier at about 4198. But at page 4199, you were -- or it was suggested to you that: "In fact, when you were interviewed in 1996, 1997, 1998 -- 1999, sorry, you never mentioned that you went to see General Gotovina on the 8th of August and discussed crimes being committed at that meeting." Subsequently, there was a discussion about the fact that that was raised or that meeting was discussed in your 2008 statement, which is Exhibit P333. And Mr. Kay asked you at page 4203: "How did it come about that you recalled it here in 2008, 12 years later, and didn't recall it earlier?" Then he asked you or suggested to you that the discussion or the -- that took place at that meeting might have been something that was suggested to you. He asked whether that was suggested to you by anyone. You indicated no. I'd just like to actually look at your earlier statements to see when you first raised what was discussed at your first meeting with General Gotovina after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection, could we look, please, at P331, the 1997 statement at page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You see that, General?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at page 18, you indicate that you had two official meetings after the war with General Gotovina. And you state at page 18: "On the first one, he clearly was elated and boasted about the Croat military success. I explained my lack of freedom of the movement. He mentioned he would look into it. I also complained about the lack of discipline of his troops, the looting and arson taking place, and the indiscriminate shooting of weapons at all times of day." Then you go on to discuss the second meeting. That was your statement in June of 1997; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, then, is it correct that later in 2008 [sic], at paragraph 7, you corrected the date of that meeting, indicating that in the 1997 statement, you had mentioned this meeting, indicating that it took place around the 12th or 13th of August. And now after reviewing the UNCRO sitreps, you wanted to correct that to indicate that the meeting actually took place on August the 8th?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn next, General, to an issue that was raised by Mr. Kay as well. That's the meeting of 24th of August, 1995 involving you, General Cermak, and Mr. Al-Alfi. And there was some discussion at pages 4227, 4228, and so on, about the discussion concerning area or area of responsibility. You recall that discussion or the questions you were asked by Mr. Kay. If I may, you referred -- Mr. Kay indicated to you in a document during your examination-in-chief to General Cermak, indicating that his area of responsibility as being vast. Then Mr. Kay turned your attention to Mr. Al-Alfi's report of the same meeting, in which Mr. Al-Alfi recorded: "In his opinion, the area is very vast and he would be lying if he told us," "he" meaning General Cermak, "nothing of the sort would continue to happen." And it goes on to referring to the issuing of orders. Then you were asked about the distinction between -- the potential distinction between area and area of responsibility. Now, in using the term "area of responsibility," General, were you attempting to convey the geographic borders of -- in which General Cermak was believed by you to be responsible and for events that were occurring?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, from my point of view, sir, it encompassed all of my sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In light of your understanding that it was his area of responsibility, were you bringing to his attention crimes that were taking place in -- for the purpose of having him address those crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the only individual that had been identified to me as responsible within my area of responsibility, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we look at D151, quickly, please. Can we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 5 toward the bottom of the page, which is Mr. Al-Alfi's report, we see the reference I just mentioned a moment ago; that is: "General Cermak making clear that in his opinion, the area is very vast," et cetera. If I could ask you, General, to turn your attention to the first sentence of that paragraph, which indicates: "We brought the continuation of burning houses and looting in the area to the attention of General Cermak and asked him to stop such acts. He accepted this fact, regarding the continuation of such incidents, and attributed them to 'persons who entered the area wearing HV uniforms and to civilians taking revenge.'" General, is that your recollection -- let me ask you: Is the reference by Mr. Al-Alfi to asking General Cermak to stop such acts where houses were being burned and looting was taking place consistent with your position as indicated in your sitrep that that encompassed his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, can I turn you next to a matter that was also raised by Mr. Kay. I'm trying to get to his matters before he has to leave, and those were matters concerning the restrictions on movement and the documents prepared by General Plestina in connection with that. I believe Mr. Kay put to you, at page 4322, that General Plestina was controlling the issue of freedom of movement between UNCRO, the UN, and the Croatian army, and you said you didn't know that. There was further discussion about that; and a line or two later or two or lines later, you indicated you don't letter whether he was in charge of controlling the issue. Then there was some further discussion about some reports by General Plestina. I'd just like to look at those reports very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call up D319. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This was shown to you during the course of that discussion, General. It's a daily report spanning the period 6th of August, 1995 until the 7th of August, 1995 to 800 hours. It indicates, among other things, that: "Our liaison officer," those are General Plestina's words, explained to you that UNCRO has complete freedom of movement regarding supply of the units on the field, "but that there is no need for their patrols, observations from their observation points, and reports on breaching the Zagreb agreement, since the situation at the moment is such that the higher authorities will decide on the potential new UNCRO task." It's correct, is isn't it, General, that by August 7th, 1995, the agreement between Mr. Sarinic and Mr. Akashi had been reached? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in paragraphs 4 and 5, that addressed issues of access by UNCRO to the civilian population for the purpose of providing humanitarian needs and also access to all areas for the purpose of carrying out surveillance, except where in the opinion of the local UNCRO military commanders, after consultation with Croatian army commanders, that the security situation doesn't permit for such surveillance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I didn't see, and I take it you did not see in this 6 to 7 August report, any reference to the is Sarinic-Akashi agreement?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean, the letter from General Plestina? The first time I saw it was when it was shown to me yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were also shown a report from the next day. That's D320, and that was a daily report from 7 August to 8 August. Again, 8 August, as you indicated -- well, let me just pause there. I can show you that document. But having reviewed it and with the permission of my colleagues, I take it you don't recall seeing any reference to the Akashi-Sarinic agreement here either?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall it was on August 8th that you received the first freedom of movement letter that was used as a pass from General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, covering the Knin and the Drnis area, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall that document was copied to two people who were General Gotovina and to Mr. Reljic?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember well it was at the bottom, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you further recall there was no copy sent to General Plestina?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not on the sheet of paper, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You testified at some length, in your examination-in-chief, about the restrictions of movement that arose during the course of August and September, and your dealings with General Cermak in connection with those restrictions of movement. Did General Cermak ever indicate to you in any way that he was consulting with or waiting for instructions from General Plestina in connection with those -- with your complaints about restrictions of movement?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you have any indication from General Cermak at all that he was beholden to or a conduit for General Plestina?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: With General Plestina, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Might we take up a matter that was raised this -- earlier today, in fact quite recently. That was at page, I think, 92 of the current transcript. That was regarding information on a sitrep from the head of the military police on, I think, August 6th, with Mr. Hill, in a document that is P351. Now, you testified, in your examination-in-chief at page 4129, about the fact that Captain Hill was allowed to go out of the compound. And the question was: "And what was it you learned from Captain Hill after he went out? Your answer was: "Well, he went out and I had asked him, you know, to have a look about the extent of the damage and what was taking place, you know, within Knin. And he came back and he reported to me in the afternoon, I think around 4.00, that he had seen extensive damage, that he had seen looting. He went to the apartment that I had occupied ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I object. This is not redirect examination. What he said and what I put to him was the sitrep that the Prosecution put into evidence, but that's not in there. It's not redirect rereading the witness' testimony two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm just about to turn it to the sitrep, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If the point is one of the discussion of the nuances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not heard any question yet. I think that for one reason or another, Mr. Tieger takes the witness back to what he said in his examination-in-chief. I don't know to what extent that's necessary, Mr. Tieger, to put the question to the witness. I see the point. Sometimes, you need to take a witness back to a certain portion of his -- If Mr. Kay would have one second. Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay, could you wait, if you would, for a second. I'll first deal with this. Sometimes, it's necessary. Sometimes it is, well, established practice to bring back to the mind of a witness what he said before, for whatever reason. I leave that open at this moment. If you can do without, that's preferred. So, therefore, the witness might have forgotten now already about what has been said. But since Mr. Kay is leaving and apparently has commitments elsewhere. Mr. Kay, I will at the end ask one question to the witness which might be of specific importance to you, which is whether the area, you remember the area of responsibility, or just the area, as we find it in the report by Mr. Al-Alfi, that the area is written with capital A; whereas, at any earlier stage in that report, we find references to the Knin area. It's again written with -- does that have any meaning for you in reading that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That it has a capital A, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me, I always use the term "area of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But if you read area with capital A, rather than without a capital, would that in this context mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't remember. Mr. Kay, since you raised the issue, I thought I would deal with it before you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... very grateful, Your Honour. With my apologies, I leave the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't want to emphasise you leaving the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, the P351 is now in front of you, the first page, and we can, if necessary, go to the portion that was discussed earlier today. That's further on in the sitrep, but I'm wondering if you can tell me what time this sitrep was prepared?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent at 1300, so it must have been prepared maybe 45 minutes to an hour before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so this, sitrep therefore, was prepared before you had spoken with Captain Hill on that day after he returned from his trip into Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to turn quickly to the 1996 statement. That's P330, I believe. And the presentation you prepared, I just had a couple of quick questions about that, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And perhaps it's more probably preferable if I turn to P401 first. Sorry, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just bring you to two quick references, hopefully, as examples. First, page 23. And if we look at the bottom paragraph of page 23, the third sentence: "General Mrksic was not there, but I met his Chief of Staff and five RSK ministers. They appeared totally confused and were mostly incoherent in their discussion or comments."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps, before leaving that document, we can turn quickly to page 34. Somehow we seem to have jumped from 33 to 35. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the third -- well, the second sentence, you indicate: "I must give credit to the initiative of my sector ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. I apologise. Is it 33 or 35?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This one is 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicate: "I must give credit to the initiative of my sector civil administrative officer, Mr. Harry Hoey; my staff; and troops for successfully managing and accommodating these refugees for an extended time."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn back to P330, and first to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, there's a reference to General Mrksic, Chief of Staff, and five RSK ministers. They appeared totally confused and in panic. There, in contrast to your presentation, is the phrase, "I don't know their names."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, again, if we could turn quickly to page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of 330, Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is a reference at the top to, again, to Harry Hoey again, the same reference that appears in the presentation, and then the added sentence: "Mr. Hoey is a British UN civilian employee, and I think he is now in Sector East." Now, General, I take it that you provided that information to the investigators; that is, the information that you did not know the names of the Mrksic's Chief of Staff and the five RSK ministers, and the information that Mr. Hoey, who was a British UN is civilian employee and who you thought was then in Sector East. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that when I say "now," that was at the time that I was speaking to those people, because when I left, he was leaving, I think, to go to Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't knows the -- I don't remember. I didn't know the Chief of Staff of the ARSK, nor the five ministers. I never met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But this would have been information that you would have provided to the investigators; that is, where Mr. Hoey was and who he was and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I object, Your Honour. I object simply because at this particular -- shortly before this time, Mr. Robertsson was in headquarters with UNCRO in Zagreb and know full well where these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. I'm just trying to understand what exactly what your problem is, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My problem is this, Judge: It goes to the source of this information at this point with regard to the inference that the General, first, if he even recalls at this time was of necessity a source of what happened to Mr. Hoey, is not exactly the full picture, given the fact that the person who was the investigator on 330 is Joakim Robertsson, who during this whole time frame was intimately aware of all these people and was working at UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question. Mr. Tieger, if you would perhaps put it again to him. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Forand, is this information that you provided to Mr. Robertsson; that is, the fact that you didn't know the names of General Mrksic's Chief of Staff and the five RSK ministers who were at the meeting and Mr. Hoey's position and whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that how the process went, that you and Mr. Robertsson would talk and he'd ask questions and you'd provide answers --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I would object to leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you put the question in a less leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did Mr. Robertsson get this information?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was asking me questions, and I was answering them, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, ultimately, were you provided with this statement which you reviewed and then signed?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you were asked some questions, I believe yesterday, by Mr. Kehoe, concerning shelling - this would be at pages 43,45 through 46, approximately - about the shelling of Strmica by HV forces, about civilians in the area. Then you were referred to an excerpt concerning a trip by Colonel Tymchuk to Strmica in late July, in which it was noted that: "There were no civilians evident in Strmica." And Mr. Kehoe asked you, at page 4346, if you knew when the civilians that had been in Strmica had left, and you indicated no. I'd like to ask you if you know why the civilians from Strmica had left by late July?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you indicated that when you arrive - and I believe this is a discussion that took place at about 4348 - you had been briefed that there were certain defensive positions in place. You had been briefed by that by your personnel travelling through the area, and I'm referring to defensive positions by the ARSK, although you hadn't seen those defensive positions yourself. Were any of those defensive positions in Knin itself, or were they elsewhere in the is sector, according to the people who briefed you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, if I remember well, I was told there was no defensive position prepared in Knin, and I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we are talking about Knin, may I take it that we're talking about the city of Knin, not the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The city, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I know that toward the end of the day today, and to some extent yesterday, you were asked some questions about orders in connection with crimes that were taking place and whether you were familiar with some orders that appear to have been reflected in documents you were shown. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents coming from who, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The documents that you were shown to you both by -- well, by Mr. Kay, I believe, yesterday, and --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I remember those documents, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you if you saw any reflection or any indication on the ground that orders to stop the crimes that were taking place had been given. Did you see a cessation or curtailment of the crimes as -- in August and early is September?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I think you can see that in the letter that I was sending to General Cermak that it was still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe asked you, before the very end of the day, about whether or not you knew of orders -- of what orders General Gotovina might have given; and you were, of course, asked yesterday about orders as well. And you were, to some extent, about other aspects of what a commander might or might not do, and I wanted to ask you this question basically, and that is: If orders such as the type that you had seen were given, and the crimes continued, is that sufficient action by a commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object, Judge. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking for a legal opinion, Mr. Tieger, I take it. At least the way in which I understand the question, you're asking for a legal opinion. If there's any factual matter in it or if you ask him what he was taught at military academy, that's a different matter. Then whether it's right, what was taught to him, is still to be seen. If you would please, so the objection is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Okay. Mr. Kehoe, I think it's a fair objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Kehoe asked you some questions about your military experience and your position as a commander, and that's the perspective from which I want to ask that question. If you, as a commander, give an order, particularly an order to stop crimes that your troops are committing, what are you expected to do based on your military experience?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What, I expect that it would be followed. If it's not followed, then I would make sure, you know, that whoever is responsible will be removed, and put somebody in place that is able to carry on the order that he has been given, and ensure that whatever has been ongoing, you know, would is stop immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the questions put in re-examination trigger the need for any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked a question about P351, and we don't need to bring it up on the screen. That is the sitrep of 1300 hours, where it was referred to Captain Hill's trip, where there is the discussion of what -- it says: "What looting there is seems to be related to beer and portable radios." You just testified that, in the afternoon, Captain Hill told you additional information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where that information that was in the sitrep came from. All I said was that this sitrep was prepared around 11.15 or 11.00, and the only time I spoke to Captain Hill was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's just bring it up, then. Exhibit 351.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, this is a sitrep of 1300 at 06 -- excuse me, on the 6th of August at 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can just have the commander's assessment - I'm just trying to get the pagination down - and if we could go two pages further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the military policemen, it notes, at 0900 was taken for a two-hour tour of Knin by HV military police: "Military police and civilian police from Split were evident in numbers and taking control of Knin. Soldiers were in the streets, and while fighting some were shooting in the air. There did not seem to be any fighting. OCMP patrol entered buildings looking for evidence of looting and destruction and found little evidence of ransacking or wanton destruction." Now, that was Captain Hill coming back and talking to you prior to 1300?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't talk to me when he came back. I spoke to him in the afternoon, and this is not the part of the commander's's assessment. That portion where -- even though I signed the whole document, that is the portion that's prepared by the OPs officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let us turn to 352, which is later on, on the 6th, at 2030 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to the last page in section F, which is the sector commander's is summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, 2030 hours, that was after you talked to Hill; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph F, you note that: "More civilians including cars with Split licence plates are seen in Knin, and a sense of normalcy is returning." Now, "a sense of normalcy," there's no discussion about looting and burning during this description of normalcy returning to Knin, is there?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. General, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Gwaunza has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: General, if I could take you back to your 1996 statement, page 10, the second paragraph. Are you there?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: You talk there about the burning of building and crops. I just want you to elaborate on the burning of the crops. Were these crops in the fields, or were these crops that had been harvested?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's crops, Your Honour, that was in the field itself. The fields were burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Was this linked to the to what you referred to on the same page -- or the third paragraph from the bottom of the page, where you talked about the fact that remote villages and peasant farms were methodically destroyed, eliminating any means of subsistence and so on.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's the same relation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If I can also take you back to your 2008 statement, paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have it with my paper here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: This is P330.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's P333, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Yes. P330, with paragraph 8. You talked there about General Gotovina acknowledging that the burning and the looting was happening, but indicating that it was something he could not control. Do you recall if he told you why he could not control?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: General Forand, I would like to refer back to your statement, P331, and page 18, line 22. You mentioned: "It seems to me that General Cermak tasks were mostly administrative." You were a person who was directly on the spot, and so this a real situation. And what was your impressions about factual authority of Mr. Cermak, whether his orders were issued to stop some criminal activities or allowed you for moment was effective or, in fact, it was not taken much in account?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously, they were not effective. Every time we met with General Cermak, as I mentioned earlier, it was very cordial. And the problem that we were giving him, you know, as far as burning, looting, he said, "Okay. I will do something about it." But to me, nothing was ever done because it carried on. And when I said that he was, for me, like an administrative type, because when I made that declaration, it was in comparison with General Gotovina who, to me, was the prototype of a soldier. And General Cermak was more of a administrator, when you compare a fighter to an administrator. So it was in that context when I used that term "administrator".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: In fact, your opinion is that his orders were not so effective at that time, and what was the reason? Did he have authority over police surveillance and remaining military forces in the area, or did he have very short authority, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, Your Honour, he was -- at least that was the impression I was getting, when we were speaking to him, that he would do something about it, but nothing was ever done. So whether he did not have the authority or not, I cannot tell you. But the only individual with whom I was and Mr. Al-Alfi was dealing with was Mr. Cermak. So, to him, we were presenting what we felt was the situation based on what our people were reporting or what the Humanity Right Action Team in Knin as they were going through their patrol were reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Forand, I have one question. You told us about one of the refugees in the compound to be your source of knowledge of how the evacuation order was communicated; that is, through the civil defence system which existed already traditionally. Now, do you happen to remember whether this was someone who learned about evacuation or evacuation orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I think, when you asked the question before, I think he said plural; the transcript was singular and then you asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not intend to use the plural, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Kehoe is correct. It's my recollection as well, Your Honour, but you can clarify with the witness. But I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there more who told you about it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do you remember whether these were people from surrounding villages from Knin or from Knin or from other specific towns?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not tell you exactly, Your Honour, if they were from Knin or other town. But it was the people that was in the camp, and they came through -- we had four or five translators which were of Serb-Croat origin, so that was one source. And these translators were also speaking a couple of weeks after the 6th to people that who were already arrived in Serbia, you know, that didn't stay in the Krajina. And it was confirmed with those people also, but I cannot tell you exactly where they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Judge Kinis put a question to you about the effectiveness of orders given by Mr. Cermak. You discussed the matters with him and you said: "I didn't see any effect."

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there were a lot of stages between discussing and orders being effective on the ground. I'd like to go with you through several stages and see whether you could comment on this stage. The first is: Are you aware of whether what Mr. Cermak said he would do, that he put that in practice?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm aware?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you say, I'll do something about it, you can say it, and did you ever learn from anyone, apart from here in the courtroom where you've seen some correspondence and some orders, did you ever learn from other persons, Cermak came to me or Cermak issued this order or anything of the kind, so that there was feedback for you that what Mr. Cermak said he would do was actually done by him.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from someone, and I'm now moving to the next stage, that he ever received anything in writing in relation to the matters you had discussed with him and where he said he would do something about it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any feedback from persons who would say: We are instructed to do this or we are requested to do this, but we are going to do things not in accordance with the instructions we received?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything else you could tell us about what you learned about the implementation, whether positive or negative, the implementation of what Mr. Cermak said he would do, apart from the documents we have seen here in court, and there's quite a number of these documents?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing to add to what has already been shown, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have the questions of the Bench raised any or have these triggered any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one brief issue, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, there was a question by Judge Gwaunza concerning burning of crops and fields. Now, the burning of the fields is, on some occasions, a demining device, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, when they were burning these fields, do you know whether they were looking for mines or not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then in relation to that last one, what they intended to do at that time, you do not know. Are you aware of mines being placed in agricultural fields.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that. I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Never any report about a mine that exploded in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only mine that I'm aware that exploded were in the Zone of Separation where we were conducting certain patrol, and that happened in July, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. Mr. Forand, although late, this concludes your testimony in this court. And I will change to French which I do understand is your native language. [Interpretation] I would really like to -- when you change to channel 5 -- could you press channel 5. I'm now speaking French. Mr. Forand, I would like to thank you to have come to The Hague and to have an answer to all the questions asked by the parties and by the Judges of the Bench, and I wish you, although belatedly, a very good return home, a good journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we could clear up the question that you posed on the beginning of the afternoon session regarding the exhibit number. You referred to the document that, in fact, has is seven pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And we were talking about a document of two pages. In fact, there is a document of seven pages in the electronic version, and it is P343.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. And the other document which has two pages only, it's P104. So I believe we are referring to the document with multiple pages, 343.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll check that. So that means that where it is on the record that the document which was not tendered at that moment, it was not admitted on the is suspicion that it was already in evidence. If it is in evidence, it will not under P104 but under P343.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, no. That is the other issue. Mr. Kuzmanovic was tendered the document and he already was given the document D329. But, in fact, that was a P104, so it's one issue. The other issue is a document with multiple pages, and that is P343. I think it's a little bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes it is. Just a bit on Friday afternoon, it's getting confused. Wouldn't it be the best way: What we are came aiming at, at that time, find out whether the document we dealt with at that time, whether that still was a need to be admitted into evidence, yes or no. We then thought that it would be already in evidence under P104. Now that seems to be not completely true. The parties are invited, or you are invited, Mr. Mikulicic, to communicate in the usual way that is through inter-parties with a copy to the legal officer, Mr. Nilsson of this Court, to explain exactly what that document we were then talking about in court whether that is in evidence; if so, where it is in evidence and whether it's one exhibit or whether it's part of a larger exhibit. Then on Monday we'll know whether there's anything to be done. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't want to -- Just very quickly, Your Honour, in light of Mr. Kay's earlier comments and the Court's suggestion that the parties alert the Court as quickly as possible to the commission of documents to be tendered across the bar in relation to a witness or testimony. I spoke to my learned friends from the Defence about this, indicated-- I was aware that we'd be receiving documents from Mr. Kay, and I indicated that we'd be tendering some bar table documents as well. So that process is underway. I just want to indicate that to the Court, and we'll try to perfect it as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's always to be preferred that if there's any relation between documents tendered from the bar table, even if not shown to the witness, but there is some relation to the content of the testimony of that witness, that they are tendered at the earliest stages, so that at least there is an opportunity to check whether those documents would trigger the need for any questions either by the other party or by the Bench to that witness. This concludes this hearing. We'll adjourn until Monday, if I'm not mistaken, the 11th of -- the 10th of June. Let me just check. Yes, I'm trying to move quicker to the recess, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn until Monday, the 9th of June, 9.00 in the morning and unfortunately Courtroom II.
